Movement Disorders 
Vol. 6, No. 1, 1991, pp. 73-75 
0 1991 Movement Disorder Society 
Brief Report 
A Therapeutic Trial of Milacemide in Myoclonus 
and the Stiff-Person Syndrome 
P. Brown, P. D. Thompson, J. C. Rothwell, B. L. Day, and C. D. Marsden 
MRC Human Movement and Balance Unit, and University Department of Clinical Neurology, Institute of 
Neurology, London, England 
Summary: We investigated the therapeutic effects of milacemide in seven patients with 
myoclonus and three patients with the stiff-person syndrome in an open-label trial. 
Milacemide was initiated at 800 mg/day and was gradually increased to a maximum 
dosage of 2,400 mg/day. No significant improvement occurred in the 10 patients. Key 
Words: Myoclonus-Stiff-person syndrome-Milacemide. 
Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS 
(1). It causes membrane hyperpolarisation and inhibits 
neuronal firing (2). Defective glycinergic systems may be 
important in animal models of spinal rigidity (3,4), and 
this has led to speculation that abnormalities of glyciner- 
gic inhibition by spinal interneurones may be important in 
the stiff-person syndrome (5). 
Several animal studies have also suggested that defec- 
tive glycinergic systems may result in myoclonus. Thus, 
the stereotactic infusion of the glycine receptor antago- 
nist, strychnine, into the medullary reticular formation 
induces generalised stimulus-sensitive myoclonus in the 
rat (6). In urea-induced myoclonus, urea has been shown 
to displace glycine at its receptor sites in the brainstem 
(7), and in DDT-induced myoclonus, intraventricular gly- 
cine is effective in suppressing the myoclonus (8). In Poll 
Hereford calves with inherited myoclonus, there is a spe- 
citic and marked deficit in strychnine binding sites in the 
spinal cord, reflecting a loss of, or defect in, glycine re- 
ceptors (9). 
Milacemide is a glycine precursor that penetrates the 
blood-brain barrier effectively, before being converted 
into glycinamide and glycine (10). It is reasonably well 
tolerated (1 1). We report an open-label trial of milacemide 
in seven patients with myoclonus of various types, and 
three patients with the stiff-person syndrome. 
Address correspondence and reprint requests to Prof. C. D. 
Marsden, University Department of Clinical Neurology, Insti- 
tute of Neurology, Queen Square, London, WClN 3BG, En- 
gland. 
PATIENTS AND METHODS 
Ten patients were enrolled in the study (Table 1). There 
were four patients (cases 14) with postanoxic multifocal 
action myoclonus. The action myoclonus was cortical in 
origin, and a cortical correlate in the backaveraged elec- 
troencephalographic activity preceded and was time- 
locked to the jerks occurring on action. Somatosensory 
evoked potentials were normal in these four patients, and 
there was no evidence of stimulus-sensitive myoclonus. 
One patient (case 5) had myoclonic dystonia. The jerks 
markedly improved with alcohol. He was the product of a 
prolonged and difficult labour. There was no relevant 
family history. There was no electrophysiological evi- 
dence that the myoclonus in this patient was cortical in 
origin. One patient (case 6) had propriospinal myoclonus 
of unknown aetiology, and has been previously reported 
(12). Another patient (case 7) had axial myoclonus and 
paroxysmal axial spasms, presumed to be propriospinal 
in origin, and has also been previously reported (P. 
Brown et al., unpublished observations). The final three 
patients (cases 8, 9, and 10) had slowly progressive axial 
stiffness, with electrophysiological evidence of continu- 
ous muscle fibre activity at rest in paraspinal muscles. All 
three patients had serological evidence of autoimmune 
disease, one patient had a history of pernicious anaemia, 
and a second had a history of insulin-dependent diabetes 
mellitus. Two of the three patients had anti-glutamic acid 
decarboxylase antibodies in the cerebrospinal fluid. The 
diagnosis of stiff-person syndrome was made in these 
three cases. All 10 patients had remained symptomatic 
despite conventional treatments. The patients gave their

The seventy of the myoclonus was rated using a mod- 
ification of the clinical rating scale described by Chad- 
wick et al. (13), and a functional assessment, which rated 
abnormalities of speech, eating, washing, dressing, and 
mobility each on a scale of 0-3. In the latter, a score of 0 
indicated normal performance, and 3 severely impaired 
performance, needing total assistance. Clinical and func- 
tional ratings, and a videotape recording of the clinical 
assessment, were made at the beginning and end of 
the study. The clinical and functional rating scores on 
treatment were expressed as percentages of the pre- 
milacemide treatment scores. A change in score on treat- 
ment with milacemide of &20% was considered as indi- 
cating no improvement, 2140% as slight improvement, 
and >41% as marked improvement. Full blood count, 
electrolytes, liver function tests, and anticonvulsant lev- 
els were also monitored at the beginning and end of the 
study in each patient. 
Treatment present at the start of the trial was kept un- 
changed during the study. Milacemide was started at 400 
mg b.d., and increased by a further 400 mg b.d. every 34 
days, up to a maximum dosage of 1,200 mg b.d. The final 
assessment was made after 3-4 days with this dosage, 
except in case 7, in whom the final assessment was made 
after 3 days with 400 mg b.d. 
RESULTS 
The clinical rating score failed to change significantly in 
the 10 patients treated with milacemide. In one patient 
(case 4), there was a mild improvement in the functional 
assessment score, but in another patient (case 3) this 
score deteriorated. 
Milacemide was generally well tolerated, although one 
case (case 10) complained of drowsiness and constipa- 
tion, and a second patient, who had epilepsy (case 4), had 
a generalised seizure during treatment. Full blood count, 
electrolytes, liver function tests, and anticonvulsant lev- 
els did not change significantly on treatment. 
DISCUSSION 
Experimental evidence in animals implicating glyciner- 
gic dysfunction in spinal rigidity (3,4) has led to trials of 
glycine in the stiff-person syndrome (14,15). These trials 
were unsuccessful, at least partly because of the weak 
penetration of the blood-brain barrier by glycine (16). 
Milacemide penetrates the blood-brain barrier well, be- 
fore being converted into glycinamide and glycine (10). 
Despite this, milacemide, up to a dosage of 2,400 mg 
daily, was ineffective in the three patients with the stiff- 
person syndrome. Most pharmacological and immunolog- 
ical evidence points to an imbalance between catechol- 
aminergic and GABAergic systems in this condition (17). 
Similarly, animal models of myoclonus, implicating gly- 
cinergic dysfunction (69) in this condition, led Truong 
and Fahn (16) to investigate the therapeutic effects of 
glycine in patients with various types of myoclonus. They 
found no evidence for an antimyoclonic action for glycine 
in doses up to 6 g per day, and again attributed this to the 
poor penetration by glycine of the blood-brain barrier. 
Movement Disorders, Vol. 6, No. 1, 1991

MILACEMIDE IN MYOCLONUS 75 
However, in the present study, milacemide also had no 
consistent effect in seven patients with myoclonus. The 
contrasting effects of milacemide treatment on the func- 
tional abilities of cases 3 and 4 were of a degree reported 
in spontaneous fluctuations by both patients. The ineffec- 
tiveness of milacemide suggests that defective glycinergic 
transmission may not be an important factor in postan- 
oxic cortical action myoclonus, myoclonic dystonia, or 
propriospinal myoclonus. Most studies of postanoxic my- 
oclonus have implicated abnormalities of serotonergic 
and GABAergic transmission (13,18). 
The apparent ineffectiveness of glycine (16) and mila- 
cemide in treating myoclonus in humans contrasts with 
the animal evidence that implicates defective glycinergic 
transmission in experimental myoclonus (6-49, and with 
the ability of milacemide to improve DDT-induced myoc- 
lonus (8). However, most of these animal experiments 
involve manipulations of the reticular formation of the 
lower brainstem, and as such, may be inappropriate mod- 
els for cortical and spinal myoclonus. The effectiveness 
of glycinergic drugs in brainstem reticular reflex myoclo- 
nus remains untested.

Wycombe, England for supplying the milacemide.
